verdict.reasoning: Patient reports: "I've really dry, itchy skin" located "All over my arms and my hands, mainly" and that it "started a few days ago."
Patient states they "went swimming a few days ago" and, when asked "did your symptoms start after you went swimming?" replies "Yes."
Rash is described as "really dry, itchy skin" and later "my skin's quite red" on "my arms and my hands." Red + itchy implies pruritic erythematous rash.

Patient says "I don't have any spots" and clinician later notes "no bleeding or discharge from skin," but cracking is only asked about ("Have you noticed any cracked skin?") and never answered. Absence of cracking is not documented.
Patient reports: "I'm using coconut butter for the past few days" and when asked if it helped the itch, answers "No."

Patient denies fever and vomiting ("No fever... No" to vomiting) and confirms urine is okay, but also says "I'm not sweating either" (not denying sweating) and explicitly denies loose stools when asked about "vomiting or loose stools." The fact incorrectly lists "diarrhea or vomiting" (duplicated vomiting) and misrepresents sweating as a denied symptom.
When asked "Do you feel tired?" patient says "Yeah, I think I have been quite tired."
Patient states "I've been drinking and eating as normal" and, when asked about bowels, replies "Yeah" and "No problems with vomiting or loose stools?" – "No."
Patient starts with "I've been really stressed at work" and later agrees work has been stressful as a teacher.

Transcript does not provide a full past medical history; patient only notes no past skin problems ("no problems of skin problems in the past"). Stating "No past medical history" overgeneralizes beyond what is discussed.
Patient says "I'm currently taking microgen" and clinician clarifies "Microgynal?" with patient confirming "Yeah," and explains it is a contraceptive pill.
When asked about allergies, patient responds "I think I might be lactose intolerant."
Clinician asks about "Food allergies, medication allergies?" and only lactose intolerance is mentioned; no drug allergies are reported, so stating none are reported is consistent with the transcript.
Patient states: "Yeah, so my dad has asthma."
In response to "who do you live with at home?" patient says "It's just me" and clinician restates "Live alone?" with patient replying "Yep."
Patient answers "No, I don't smoke" to smoking, "No" to alcohol, and denies recreational drugs when asked.
Patient confirms "I work as a teacher" and later "Yes, that's right" to being a primary school teacher; work is described as stressful due to the children.

Symptoms: "really dry, itchy skin" that is "quite red" on hands and arms after swimming; clinician states "I wonder whether you may have something called dermatitis," consistent with pruritic erythematous rash likely contact/irritant dermatitis post pool exposure.

Patient describes work as stressful and that the kids "have been really annoying"; clinician notes stress can be a contributing factor. Describing this as mild work-related stress is a reasonable inference and not contradicted.
Clinician says "We have steroid creams I can give you" but does not specify duration "for 5 to 7 days." The explicit time frame is not in the transcript.
Clinician explains emollients "which can help with the dry skin" and instructs "paste onto your skin throughout the day for the next few days," aligning with liberal daytime use.
Clinician advises: "You can also try antihistamines, so you can get things over the counter. Pyritin, loratadine. That can sometimes help with the itchiness."
Clinician explicitly states: "Paracetamol on this occasion wouldn't be helpful. Painkillers wouldn't be helpful on this occasion."
Although stress is discussed during the consultation, there is no explicit plan stated to re-address stress at follow-up; follow-up is framed around the rash and symptoms.

Clinician advises: "if it's still not getting better, come back and see me next week and we can have another look again at your symptoms," which corresponds to follow up next week if no improvement or worsening.
